chapter: Willie Lynch, the Blue Rhythm Band and Teddy Hill
title: Dancing schools and taxi dance halls: why musicians learned to read
summary: Many players learned reading in ten-cents-a-dance halls, playing stock arrangements chorus by chorus for fifty-five minutes an hour, which gave Holmes no inspiration.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: But you said a lot of these men who were in the band now had come out of dancing schools or taxi dance halls...
Yes, they could read. Men like Damian Moon... Moon didn't miss nothin'. He could read anything you put up there.
And Greely was a good reader.
Well, Greely was a good reader anyway. I don't think Greely ever worked in a dancing school. But he was a good reader. He was a violinist before he was a
saxophone player. Most violinists that studied violin, they are good readers.
Well, that goes for... When you came here, you said Johnny Russell and Edgar Sampson were here...
Mmm-hmm.
...and they were violinists, too.
They were violinists, and all of them worked in dancing schools, too. You know what I mean? So there you go! Beside being a violinist, they would have still been good readers anyway.
But describe a dancing school or a taxi dance hall. Why was there so much reading?
Well, that's the way it was operated. The band would play... They would have what you call stock arrangements. You know what a stock arrangement is.
Yeah.

And they'd have a book about that thick with music. The way they used to play... The girls would get you a ticket. You'd play one chorus, and stop. She gets another ticket. When you stop, every time you stop they get a ticket. Maybe they play two choruses.
And this is what comes from that "ten cents a dance."
That's what it is! That's what it is. They called them "dancing schools" and then they called them

"taxi dance halls" and "ten cents a dance" -- they had a lot of names. The band would play... In fact, we were finishing up a number now, [DUH/DUH-DE-DUH-DE/DUP-DUP], one-two, into the next number -- here comes another ticket. And that's the way they played. Fifty-five minutes continuously, five minutes rest out of an hour. And they would work. I don't know how many hours they worked in them places, but they worked hard. I mean, you know...
So most of the time there was no original music. It was just stock after stock after stock.

Stock after stock, or anything they wanted to play. One of them head numbers, something like that. They'd make up something, 32 bars, and get it...so she could get a ticket for the dance. And I mean, you're playing the music, so you're playing fifty-five minutes of music each and every night. And say, it's nobody on the floor -- nobody dancing. You still have to play to an empty place. Well, you know how much inspiration you can get out of an empty ballroom, nobody on the floor, the girls are down on the other end there talking about this-that-and-the-other and one thing or another, and nobody on the dance floor -- and you're playing. So I mean, where is the inspiration? You know, there's nothin' then. Well, I mean, you got so you'd just automatically make some noise on ...(?)...

That's why I always tried to stay away from them. There was no inspiration for me. And I had to be inspired when I played. That's why I never went in too much for playing clubs and things where they sit down and drink and look at you. That to me was for the birds. I like to see people dancing, payin' attention to each other. Don't pay no attention to me. Pay attention to each other, dance and enjoy yourself. That's the kind of playing I like to do.
